title: npm Staged Publishing Available, Adding a Human Approval Step Before Packages Go Live
gist: GitHub-maintained npm has shipped staged publishing generally available: a publish now uploads a tarball to a stage queue that a human maintainer must approve with a 2FA challenge before consumers can install it, explicitly aimed at killing CI-takeover publish attacks like the Shai-Hulud worm waves. pnpm, Yarn and release-it have already cloned the subcommands within one release cycle, while practitioners argue over whether an opt-in control that depends on maintainer diligence is a real fix or only slows the spread rate.

insights.claim: npm's staged publishing splits package release into two steps: the prebuilt tarball is uploaded to a stage queue visible on npmjs.com and in the CLI, and a human maintainer must pass a two-factor authentication challenge before the version becomes installable.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: The registry's trust boundary moves from 'whoever holds the token' to 'whoever holds the second factor at approval time' — the key design pattern any package registry or internal artifact store will now be benchmarked against.
insights.quote: Instead of a direct publish that immediately exposes a version to consumers, the prebuilt tarball is uploaded to a stage queue that is visible both on npmjs.com and in the CLI.
insights.locator: npm, the default package manager for Node.js

insights.claim: Staging a package on npm deliberately requires no 2FA and works with any token type, so non-interactive CI pipelines keep publishing unchanged while the proof-of-presence requirement shifts entirely onto the approval step.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: This is the adoption unlock: security is added without breaking automated release pipelines, which is why uptake could be far faster than past npm security mandates.
insights.quote: Staging itself does not require 2FA and works with any token type, so non-interactive CI pipelines are unaffected, and the proof of presence moves to the approval step.
insights.locator: Instead of a direct publish that immediately exposes

insights.claim: npm staged publishing has hard version floors — npm CLI 11.15.0 or newer and Node 22.14.0 or higher — and only works for packages that already exist on the registry, so it cannot protect a first-time publish.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Toolchain floors gate real-world coverage: organisations pinned to older Node or CLI versions get zero protection until they upgrade, and brand-new package names remain an open attack surface.
insights.quote: The feature requires npm CLI 11.15.0 or newer and Node 22.14.0 or higher, and the package must already exist on the registry.

insights.claim: The staged publishing surface is a five-verb workflow — npm stage publish, list, view, approve and reject — with approve prompting for 2FA and flags such as --tag and --provenance behaving exactly as they do for npm publish.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: A deliberately tiny, familiar API is what makes this cheap to adopt and trivially copyable by rival package managers — which is precisely what happened.
insights.quote: npm stage approve <stage-id> # promote it to the registry, prompts for 2FA
insights.locator: The workflow is a small set of subcommands

themes.theme: OIDC trusted publishing as the intended pairing

insights.claim: GitHub recommends pairing staged publishing with trusted publishing over OIDC and allows a configuration to be limited to stage only, so a direct npm publish from that workflow is rejected outright.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: The stage-only OIDC config is the actual hardening primitive: it makes a compromised CI workflow structurally incapable of shipping to consumers, not merely discouraged from doing so.
insights.quote: GitHub recommends pairing staging with trusted publishing over OIDC, where a configuration can be limited to stage only, so a direct npm publish from that workflow is rejected outright.
insights.locator: GitHub recommends pairing staging with trusted publishing

insights.claim: Teams already running bulk trusted publishing configuration can reuse it to migrate packages to staging, reducing the change to a CLI upgrade and a swapped publish command.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Low migration cost for the organisations that already invested in trusted publishing — a compounding advantage for GitHub's earlier supply-chain groundwork.
insights.locator: Teams already using bulk trusted publishing configuration

insights.claim: GitHub's stated roadmap is to default 2FA-bypassing granular access tokens to stage only and to add an allowScripts field that flips install scripts to opt-in in npm v12.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Install scripts are the primary worm propagation vector; making them opt-in at v12 is a larger structural break than staging itself and will force build-tooling rework across the ecosystem.
insights.quote: GitHub says next steps include defaulting 2FA-bypassing granular access tokens to stage only, and an allowScripts field that flips install scripts to opt-in in v12.

insights.claim: The same npm release adds --allow-file, --allow-remote and --allow-directory alongside the existing --allow-git, each accepting all or none and configurable in .npmrc or package.json, with --allow-git defaulting to none in v12.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: A quiet tightening of dependency-source permissions that will break installs relying on git or file dependencies once v12 flips the default — worth auditing lockfiles now.

themes.theme: Supply-chain incident pressure as the forcing function

insights.claim: npm shipped staged publishing against a backdrop the author characterises as a punishing run of supply chain incidents, from the Shai-Hulud worm waves to a rocky migration off classic tokens.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Registry security features are now incident-driven rather than roadmap-driven; expect the cadence of breaking security defaults to track attack frequency, not release planning.
insights.quote: The context is a punishing run of supply chain incidents, from the Shai-Hulud worm waves to a rocky migration off classic tokens.
insights.locator: The context is a punishing run

insights.claim: Security researcher Adnan Khan publicly urged every npm publisher to enable staged publishing immediately, framing publish-from-CI-via-OIDC plus human approval as a direct denial of the Shai-Hulud attack pattern.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Unqualified endorsement from the researcher community is the strongest available adoption catalyst — watch for it becoming a de facto audit expectation for maintainers.
insights.quote: Everyone publishing to NPM should turn this feature on today.
insights.locator: Security researcher Adnan Khan was unequivocal

insights.claim: A dissenting Hacker News commenter, weinzierl, argued that staged publishing is at best a band aid and that in the long run it will actively hurt efforts toward more secure infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: The against-consensus risk is moral hazard: a visible control that satisfies auditors can crowd out deeper fixes like reproducible builds or default script sandboxing.
insights.quote: Seen favorably, staged publishing is a band aid. Seen more realistically I believe that in the long run it will even hurt our efforts for more secure infra.

insights.claim: The counter-argument is that when combined with trusted publishing, staging is not a band-aid but eliminates an entire class of CI takeover publish attacks, closing a large gap even if attackers find other routes.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Frames the correct evaluation metric: judge the control by which attack class it deletes, not by whether it makes the ecosystem safe overall.
insights.quote: For trusted publishing, it's not a band-aid, it's a significant improvement that kills an entire class of CI takeover publish attacks.

insights.claim: Practitioners flagged the core weakness as opt-in adoption — one commenter noted it only helps "if maintainers actually use it" and another asked whether it should be enforced by default — while a Reddit commenter framed the benefit as a reduction in spread rate rather than a cure.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: The real signal to track is not the feature launch but the enforcement date — voluntary controls in the npm ecosystem have historically converted slowly until made mandatory.
insights.locator: Others questioned adoption, with turkeyboi noting

themes.theme: Rival package managers converge within one cycle

insights.claim: Competing JavaScript package managers matched npm's staging within a release cycle: pnpm 11.3 added pnpm stage with the same subcommands, Yarn exposes yarn npm stage list, and release-it supports a "stage": true option.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Instant cross-tool convergence means staged publishing becomes an ecosystem-wide baseline expectation, not a GitHub lock-in feature — reducing npm's differentiation from the change it shipped.

insights.claim: pnpm layers a complementary defence on top of staging by delaying installation of very new releases by default, attacking the same worm-propagation window from the consumer side rather than the publisher side.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Publisher-side approval and consumer-side cooldown are separable controls; defence-in-depth here means the effective attack window is the intersection, not either measure alone.
insights.quote: pnpm also delays installing very new releases by default, a complementary defence.
